subject: Chemistry
description: Saponification, micelles, hard water issues, detergent advantages, biodegradability

questions.stem: The chemical reaction by which soap is manufactured (alkali + fat → soap + glycerol) is called:
questions.explanation: Saponification — alkaline hydrolysis of triglyceride (fat or oil) to give soap (sodium / potassium salt of fatty acid) + glycerol. Reagents: NaOH gives 'hard' soaps (bar soap); KOH gives 'soft' soaps (liquid hand soap, shaving soaps). Fats from oils — palm, coconut, olive, tallow. Industrial process: 'hot process' (heat + lye, faster) or 'cold process' (room temperature, slower 4-6 weeks for cure). Glycerol is a valuable byproduct (used in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: A soap molecule is described as 'amphiphilic' — meaning it has:

options.option_text: A hydrophobic (water-hating) hydrocarbon tail AND a hydrophilic (water-loving) ionic head

questions.explanation: Soap = sodium salt of long-chain fatty acid, e.g., sodium stearate CH₃(CH₂)₁₆COO⁻Na⁺. Long hydrocarbon tail (~12-18 C) is hydrophobic / lipophilic; ionic carboxylate head is hydrophilic. In water, molecules form MICELLES — spherical clusters with tails pointing inward (trapping oil/dirt) and heads facing outward (water-soluble). This is how soap removes greasy dirt — the dirt gets emulsified inside micelles and washes away.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Soap does NOT lather well with HARD water because:

options.option_text: Hard water dissolves the soap completely
Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions react with soap to form an insoluble scum
Hard water destroys the hydrocarbon tail

questions.explanation: Hard water contains Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ from dissolved CaCO₃ / MgCO₃ / sulphates / chlorides. These react with soap (RCOO⁻Na⁺) to form Ca(RCOO)₂ / Mg(RCOO)₂ — INSOLUBLE 'scum' (curdy white precipitate). So most soap is wasted before any lather forms. Detergents (synthetic surfactants) overcome this — their Ca/Mg salts are soluble. Also softening hard water (adding Na₂CO₃ — washing soda; or ion-exchange resins) is a fix.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Synthetic detergents are advantageous over soaps mainly because:

options.option_text: They work even in hard water and acidic conditions

questions.explanation: Detergents contain sulphonate (-SO₃⁻) or sulphate (-OSO₃⁻) hydrophilic heads instead of carboxylate. Their Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ salts are SOLUBLE — no scum in hard water. Also work in acidic conditions (where soap precipitates out as the free fatty acid). Drawback — many older 'branched-chain' detergents (alkyl benzene sulphonates) are non-biodegradable, polluting waterways. Modern 'linear' alkyl sulphonates + biological enzyme additives are biodegradable + greener. Look for 'eco-friendly' label.

questions.stem: The pH of normal household soap solution is typically:
questions.explanation: Soap is a salt of a strong base (NaOH/KOH) + weak acid (long-chain fatty acid). Hydrolyses in water to give a slightly alkaline solution (pH ~9-10) — explains the slippery feel. Strongly alkaline soap (>pH 11) can be irritating to skin. Some skin-friendly soaps (Dove, Pears) are formulated to be 'mild' (pH ~7). Detergents are usually pH 7-10. Indicator like phenolphthalein turns pink in soap solution (pH > 8.3 trigger).

questions.stem: What component is mainly added to make soaps appear opaque + 'milky'?
questions.explanation: TiO₂ — high refractive index → scatters light → opaque white appearance. Used in toothpastes, paints, sunscreens, foods (E171, though now banned in EU since 2022 over health concerns) for the same reason. Other soap additives: sodium silicate (water glass — makes the bar harder), glycerine (humectant for skin softness), perfumes, antibacterials (triclosan was banned by US FDA in 2016 for OTC washes), pumice/oat for exfoliating soaps, dyes for colour. Transparent soaps use sugar/alcohol to dissolve crystallisation.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Cleansing action of soap relies on the formation of:

options.option_text: Micelles trapping oil/dirt in their hydrophobic core

questions.explanation: Above the Critical Micelle Concentration (CMC), surfactant molecules cluster into spherical structures called micelles. Hydrophobic tails point inward, trapping oily dirt; hydrophilic heads face outward into water. The micelle (with its dirt cargo) is washable. Without surfactants, oil + water don't mix. CMC for SDS (sodium dodecyl sulphate, common detergent) ≈ 8 mM. Below CMC — soap behaves as individual molecules, no cleaning action.
